property_holder: Steward, in his land and the tree on it
challenger: Fisher and Parmele, asserting a claim to the honey
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the landowner's interest by ruling that the plaintiffs' actions constituted a trespass and did not create a property right in the honey.
principle: Ownership of land generally includes ownership of wild animals and their products found on that land, especially against a trespasser.
doctrines: Occupancy; Trespass; Ratione Soli; Local Custom

court: New York Supreme Court of Judicature
property_holder: mixed
challenger: Pierson (claiming the fox by capture)
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that Post, the initial pursuer, had not established a property interest in the fox, thus Pierson's capture was legitimate.
principle: Property rights in wild animals are generally acquired through actual physical possession or by depriving the animal of its natural liberty, not merely by pursuit.
doctrines: Rule of Capture; Occupancy; Ferae Naturae

court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: The United States, in the land granted to McIntosh
challenger: Johnson and Graham's Lessee, asserting title from Indian tribes
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the U.S. government's title, derived from discovery and conquest, over claims based on direct purchase from Native American tribes.
principle: The principle of discovery grants exclusive title to the discovering sovereign, limiting the property rights of indigenous populations to occupancy and denying their power to alienate land to private individuals.
doctrines: Discovery Doctrine; Governmental Pre-emption; Indian Right of Occupancy

case_name: Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge
court: Supreme Court of the United States
plaintiff: The Proprietors of the Charles River Bridge
defendant: The Proprietors of the Warren Bridge
property_holder: The Proprietors of the Charles River Bridge, in their chartered right to operate a toll bridge
challenger: The Proprietors of the Warren Bridge, authorized by the state to build a competing bridge
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the original charter did not explicitly grant an exclusive right, thus allowing the state to authorize a competing bridge.
principle: The state's power to promote public welfare through new infrastructure is paramount, and grants of corporate privileges are strictly construed against implied exclusivity.
doctrines: Contract Clause; Strict Construction of Public Grants; State Sovereignty; Eminent Domain

property_holder: Clark, in the logs he found
challenger: the Maloneys, as subsequent finders
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the first finder's special property interest against a subsequent finder.
principle: The first finder of lost chattel establishes a special property right that is superior to any subsequent finder, even if the first finder loses possession.
doctrines: Finder's Rights; Prior Possession; Special Property

property_holder: Merriweather, in the usufructuary right to water flowing through his land
challenger: Evans, by diverting the water upstream
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected Merriweather's right to the reasonable use of the water against Evans's complete diversion.
principle: Riparian rights to water are based on reasonable use, balancing the needs of all landowners along a stream, with natural wants prioritized over artificial ones.
doctrines: Riparian Rights; Reasonable Use Doctrine; Natural vs. Artificial Wants

property_holder: The borough of Stamford, in the fee of the land where the manure lay
challenger: Haslem, who claimed a right to the manure by labor and first possession
owner_prevailed_why: The court found the manure was abandoned personal property and the borough had no objection to its removal.
principle: Labor invested in abandoned property can establish a temporary right of possession, protected for a reasonable time, even against those who would otherwise claim it by prior possession.
doctrines: First Occupancy; Abandonment; Labor and Value Enhancement; Reasonable Time for Removal

property_holder: Green, Camp, and Brooks, in the standing timber
challenger: Wetherbee, asserting title to the hoops
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the value added by the defendant's labor in good faith was so great that title to the transformed goods passed to him.
principle: When a party in good faith substantially transforms another's property into a much more valuable and different article, the original owner may lose title to the transformed item and be limited to monetary damages for the original value.
doctrines: Accession; Good Faith; Relative Values

property_holder: Campbell et al., in their land and improvements
challenger: Seaman, asserting a right to operate his brick-yard
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the plaintiffs' interest in the quiet enjoyment of their property by enjoining the defendant's brick-making operation.
principle: Property rights include the right to quiet enjoyment of one's land, and this right can be protected by injunction against activities on neighboring land that cause substantial and irreparable harm, even if those activities are otherwise lawful.
doctrines: Nuisance; Irreparable Injury; Prescriptive Right; Acquiescence

property_holder: Edwards, in his land
challenger: Allouez Mining Co., by depositing sand on his land
owner_prevailed_why: The court denied the property owner's request for an injunction, finding that his speculative motives and the availability of damages meant he was not entitled to equitable relief.
principle: Equitable remedies like injunctions are discretionary and may be denied if the plaintiff's motives are speculative and monetary damages provide adequate compensation, especially when granting the injunction would cause disproportionate hardship to the defendant.
doctrines: Injunctive Relief; Balancing of Equities; Irreparable Injury; Adequate Remedy at Law

court: United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts
property_holder: Ghen, in the whale he killed
challenger: Rich, as the buyer from the finder
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected Ghen's claim to the whale based on established custom and the impracticality of traditional first possession rules.
principle: Customary practices within an industry can establish property rights when they are reasonable, long-standing, and necessary for the industry's viability.
doctrines: First Possession; Customary Law; Rule of Capture

case_name: Coffin v. Left Hand Ditch Co.
property_holder: Coffin et al., in their riparian land rights
challenger: Left Hand Ditch Co., asserting prior appropriation of water
owner_prevailed_why: The court rejected the traditional riparian rights of the landowners in favor of the prior appropriator's claim to water.
principle: In regions where water is scarce, the right to water is determined by the priority of its beneficial appropriation, rather than by riparian land ownership.
doctrines: Prior Appropriation Doctrine; Riparian Rights; Beneficial Use

property_holder: Goddard, in his land
challenger: Winchell, asserting a claim to the aerolite as a finder
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that the aerolite became part of the land and thus belonged to the landowner.
principle: Property embedded in the earth through natural processes is considered part of the land and belongs to the landowner, rather than being subject to finder's rules.
doctrines: Accession; Quicquid plantatur solo, solo cedit; Finder's Rights; Realty vs. Chattel

property_holder: The unknown owner of Section 22, in their land and the logs cut from it.
challenger: Sigfrid Anderson, who cut the logs and possessed them.
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the possessor's interest against a subsequent wrongdoer, not the true owner's interest.
principle: Possession, even if wrongfully obtained, creates a superior right against subsequent wrongdoers who cannot demonstrate a better title or connection to the true owner.
doctrines: Relative Title; Possession as Title; Replevin

court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Nebraska, in its original territory bounded by the Missouri River
challenger: Iowa, asserting a claim to land based on the river's new course
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected Nebraska's original boundary by ruling that avulsion does not change the boundary line.
principle: Boundaries defined by a river shift with gradual changes (accretion) but remain fixed in the old channel after a sudden change (avulsion).
doctrines: Accretion; Avulsion; Riparian Rights

case_name: Illinois Central Railroad Co. v. Illinois
court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: State of Illinois, in the submerged lands of Lake Michigan
challenger: Illinois Central Railroad Company, asserting ownership via legislative grant
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the state could not alienate its public trust over the submerged lands of Lake Michigan to a private corporation.
principle: States hold navigable waters and the lands beneath them in an inalienable public trust, which cannot be substantially alienated to private parties.
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine; Equal Footing Doctrine; Riparian Rights; Police Power

property_holder: Pile et al., in their land
challenger: Pedrick et al., with their encroaching foundation
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the landowner's right to exclude by ordering the removal of the encroachment.
principle: A landowner's right to exclude others from their property is a fundamental right that can compel the removal of even minor, unintentional encroachments.
doctrines: Trespass; Right to Exclude; Equitable Remedies

class_topic: Criminal Law, Self-Help & Common Law Defenses
property_holder: Putnam, in his dock
challenger: Ploof, asserting a right to moor due to necessity
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that the property owner's right to exclude was limited by the necessity doctrine, allowing the plaintiff to moor to the dock.
principle: The right to exclude is not absolute and can be limited by the doctrine of necessity, especially to preserve life and property.
doctrines: Necessity Doctrine; Trespass; Scope of Employment

court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
property_holder: Pardee et al, in their land with standing timber
challenger: Camden Lumber Company, by cutting timber
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the landowners' interest by allowing an injunction to prevent the destruction of their timber, finding damages inadequate.
principle: Property owners have a right to preserve the unique character of their land, and equity will intervene to protect this right when legal remedies are inadequate.
doctrines: Injunction; Adequacy of Legal Remedy; Irreparable Injury; Standing Timber

case_name: International News Service v. Associated Press
court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Associated Press, in the news it gathered
challenger: International News Service, by appropriating and reselling the news
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected AP's interest in the news it gathered by enjoining INS's misappropriation.
principle: Courts may create new property-like rights to protect the labor and investment of a party against unfair competition, even for things not traditionally considered property.
doctrines: quasi-property; unfair competition; misappropriation; abandonment

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
property_holder: Cowen, in the Oregon and California Railroad bond
challenger: Pressprich, by misdelivering the bond
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected Cowen's interest by holding Pressprich strictly liable for the misdelivery of the bond.
principle: An involuntary bailee who exercises dominion over property becomes strictly liable for its misdelivery.
doctrines: Involuntary Bailment; Conversion; Strict Liability; Dominion

court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Pennsylvania Coal Co., in its reserved right to mine coal
challenger: Mahon, asserting rights under the Kohler Act
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the coal company's reserved property interest by ruling the state act an unconstitutional taking.
principle: Government regulation that severely diminishes the economic viability of a property right can constitute a regulatory taking, requiring compensation under the Fifth Amendment.
doctrines: Regulatory Taking; Police Power; Diminution in Value; Takings Clause

property_holder: McLean, in his lot
challenger: Sanborn, asserting a reciprocal negative easement
owner_prevailed_why: The court enforced an implied restriction against the owner's desired use of their property.
principle: Property restrictions can be implied and enforced in equity based on a common development scheme and notice, even if not explicitly stated in a deed.
doctrines: Reciprocal Negative Easement; Constructive Notice; Equitable Servitude

case_name: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.
court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Ambler Realty Company, in its undeveloped land
challenger: The Village of Euclid, through its zoning ordinance
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld the zoning ordinance, which restricted the owner's desired use of its land and reduced its value.
principle: Government regulation of land use through zoning is a legitimate exercise of police power, provided it is not arbitrary or unreasonable and serves the public welfare.
doctrines: Police Power; Zoning; Due Process; Nuisance

property_holder: Edwards, in his land and cave
challenger: Lee, asserting a claim of trespass under his land
owner_prevailed_why: The court allowed a temporary invasion of the property holder's land for a survey, despite the owner's objection.
principle: Courts can compel temporary invasions of private property for discovery purposes in litigation, balancing traditional ownership rights with the need for justice.
doctrines: Ad Coelum Doctrine; Writ of Prohibition; Equity Power to Order Inspection; Irreparable Injury

property_holder: Isaac V. Brokaw's estate, in the residence at 1 East 79th Street
challenger: George Tuttle Brokaw, the life tenant
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the original character of the property as devised by the testator, preventing the life tenant from making fundamental changes.
principle: The principle of waste prevents a life tenant from making fundamental alterations to property that change its character, even if economically beneficial, to preserve the inheritance for remaindermen.
doctrines: Waste; Life Estate; Remainderman's Rights

court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
defendant: Pacific Air Transport; United Air Lines Transport Corporation
property_holder: Hinman et al., in their land and claimed superjacent airspace
challenger: commercial airlines flying through the airspace
owner_prevailed_why: The court limited the landowner's property interest in airspace to actual use and enjoyment, finding no trespass without actual damage.
principle: Property rights in airspace are not absolute and extend only to what a landowner can reasonably use in connection with their land, balancing individual ownership with public utility.
doctrines: Ad Coelum Doctrine; Airspace Ownership; Trespass

property_holder: Bakers, in their farm
challenger: Howard County Hunt, asserting a right to hunt across the land
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Bakers' right to exclude and peacefully enjoy their property by granting an injunction against repeated trespasses.
principle: Property owners have a right to peaceful enjoyment of their land, and equity will intervene with an injunction to prevent repeated trespasses when legal remedies are inadequate.
doctrines: Trespass by Animals; Injunction for Repeated Trespasses; Adequacy of Legal Remedy; Self-Defense of Property

case_name: Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank
property_holder: Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank, in its fee simple interest in the land
challenger: Neponsit Property Owners' Association, asserting a lien based on a covenant
owner_prevailed_why: The court enforced the covenant against the property owner, requiring payment for common area maintenance.
principle: Courts will interpret the requirements for covenants running with the land flexibly to give effect to the parties' intent and the practical benefits of the covenant for a community.
doctrines: Covenants Running with the Land; Touch and Concern; Privity of Estate; Affirmative Covenants

case_name: Medico-Dental Building Co. v. Horton & Converse
plaintiff: Medico-Dental Building Company of Los Angeles
property_holder: Medico-Dental Building Company, in the building
challenger: Horton & Converse, asserting a right to exclusive use
owner_prevailed_why: The court found the landlord breached a material covenant, justifying the tenant's rescission of the lease.
principle: Lease covenants can be dependent, allowing a tenant to rescind the lease if a landlord materially breaches a covenant that goes to the entire consideration of the agreement.
doctrines: Dependent Covenants; Material Breach; Lease as Contract; Waiver

court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Miller et al., in their land
challenger: the United States, asserting eminent domain
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that the landowners were not entitled to an increase in value due to the government's project.
principle: The principle of just compensation in eminent domain aims to indemnify the owner for their loss, not to allow them to profit from the government's need or project.
doctrines: Just Compensation; Market Value; Eminent Domain; Project-Enhanced Value

property_holder: Strain, as the buyer of the house
challenger: Green, who removed items from the house
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the buyer's interest by ruling that the removed items were fixtures and part of the real estate.
principle: The determination of whether an item is a fixture depends on objective factors of annexation, adaptation, and intent, not the secret subjective intent of the annexor.
doctrines: fixtures; objective intent; annexation

property_holder: Olwell, in his egg-washing machine
challenger: Nye & Nissen Company, by unauthorized use
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the owner's right to exclusive use by allowing recovery of the tortfeasor's profits from unauthorized use.
principle: Property rights include the right to exclusive use, and unauthorized use can lead to restitution of the user's profits, even if the owner suffered no direct loss.
doctrines: unjust_enrichment; waiver_of_tort; restitution; right_to_exclusive_use

court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Shelley, in his purchased property
challenger: Kraemer, asserting the restrictive covenant
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Shelleys' right to occupy their purchased property by ruling against the enforcement of the restrictive covenant.
principle: The state cannot use its judicial power to enforce private agreements that violate the constitutional rights of individuals, particularly the right to equal protection.
doctrines: State Action Doctrine; Equal Protection Clause; Racially Restrictive Covenants

property_holder: Rylands and Reid, in their land
challenger: Golden Press, Inc., with its encroaching footings
owner_prevailed_why: The court prioritized the defendant's hardship over the plaintiffs' right to exclude the minor encroachment.
principle: Courts may balance the equities and deny a mandatory injunction for a minor encroachment if the cost of removal is disproportionate to the harm, especially if the encroachment was unintentional.
doctrines: Mandatory Injunction; Balancing of Equities; Relative Hardship; Encroachment

property_holder: Jaber, in his leasehold interest
challenger: Miller, asserting the transfer was a sublease
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that Jaber's transfer was an assignment, upholding his right to collect the deferred payments.
principle: Courts may prioritize the intent of the parties over rigid, outdated common law distinctions when determining the nature of a property transfer.
doctrines: Assignment; Sublease; Intent of Parties; Feudal Tenures

chapter: 8. Title Records and the Transfer of Property
class_topic: Title & Transfer: Land Transactions, Good Faith Purchasers & Recording
property_holder: Hauck, in his mineral rights
challenger: White and Duncan, as subsequent purchasers
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the original grantor's potential negligence could prevent him from recovering the property from a bona fide purchaser, even if the original deed was void.
area: 8. Title Records and the Transfer of Property
principle: While fraud in the execution renders a deed void between original parties, a grantor's negligence in signing may prevent recovery against a bona fide purchaser, balancing protection for original owners against the security of transactions.
doctrines: Fraud in the Execution; Void vs. Voidable; Bona Fide Purchaser; Estoppel

property_holder: Harbison, in his cooperage business and property
challenger: City of Buffalo, asserting its zoning ordinance
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the city could terminate the nonconforming use if the amortization period was reasonable, remanding for a factual determination.
principle: Zoning ordinances can require the termination of existing nonconforming uses after a reasonable period, balancing public welfare against private investment.
doctrines: Nonconforming Use; Amortization; Police Power; Vested Rights

case_name: Fontainebleau Hotel Corp. v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five Inc.
property_holder: Fontainebleau Hotel Corp., in its land
challenger: Forty-Five Twenty-Five Inc., asserting a right to light and air
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Fontainebleau's right to build on its land, finding no legal right to light and air for the Eden Roc.
principle: Landowners generally have the right to develop their property without regard to a neighbor's access to light and air, absent specific legal restrictions.
doctrines: Right to light and air; Spite structures; Ancient lights; Sic utere tuo ut alienum non laedas

case_name: Producers Lumber & Supply Co. v. Olney Building Co.
property_holder: Producers Lumber & Supply Company, Inc., in Lot 8
challenger: Olney Building Company, asserting a claim to the improvements it built
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the landowner's interest by holding the improver liable for the value of the destroyed dwelling.
principle: Self-help by an improver, even a good-faith one, can lead to liability for waste and forfeiture of equitable claims.
doctrines: Fixtures; Good Faith Improver; Waste; Unclean Hands

case_name: Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82 v. Toscano
court: Court of Appeal of the State of California
plaintiff: Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82, Independent Order of Odd Fellows
property_holder: Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82, in fee simple
challenger: The estates of the grantors, asserting a right of reverter
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld the grantors' right to impose a use restriction that could lead to reverter, limiting the lodge's ownership.
principle: Conditions restricting the use of land, even if they indirectly limit who can use it, are generally valid and severable from void restraints on alienation.
doctrines: Restraints on Alienation; Fee Simple Subject to Condition Subsequent; Severability of Conditions; Intent of Grantor

property_holder: Jost and other farmers, in their land and crops
challenger: Dairyland Power Cooperative, through its emissions
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the property owners were entitled to compensation for damages caused by the nuisance, regardless of the defendant's due care or the utility of its operations.
principle: Property owners have a right to be free from substantial interference with the use and enjoyment of their land, and this right is protected by damages even if the interfering activity is socially beneficial and conducted with due care.
doctrines: Nuisance; Due Care in Nuisance Actions; Balancing Utility vs. Harm; Substantial Injury

case_name: State ex rel. Thornton v. Hay
property_holder: Hay, in the dry-sand area of their ocean-front property
challenger: The State, asserting public recreational rights
owner_prevailed_why: The court recognized a public easement over the Hays' private property based on custom, limiting their right to exclude.
principle: Long-standing public custom can establish an easement for public use over private land, overriding a landowner's right to exclude.
doctrines: Customary Rights; Public Easement; Jus Publicum

property_holder: Howard, in the disputed land
challenger: Kunto, asserting adverse possession
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the Kuntos and their predecessors had met the requirements for adverse possession, defeating Howard's record title.
principle: Adverse possession rules, particularly regarding continuity and privity for tacking, are interpreted flexibly to account for the nature of the property and good-faith reliance on mistaken deed descriptions.
doctrines: Adverse Possession; Tacking; Privity; Continuity of Possession

case_name: Javins v. First National Realty Corp.
court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
plaintiff: Ethel Javins, Rudolph Saunders, Stanley Gross
property_holder: First National Realty Corporation, in its apartment buildings
challenger: tenants asserting housing code violations
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the landlord's property interest was subject to an implied warranty of habitability, which the tenants could use as a defense.
principle: The court recognized that residential leases are primarily contracts for shelter, implying a warranty of habitability that requires landlords to maintain premises in accordance with housing codes.
doctrines: Implied Warranty of Habitability; Contractual Interdependence; Caveat Emptor (Rejected); Housing Code Violations

defendant: George Nickolaus et al. (City of Columbia)
property_holder: Higday et al., in the percolating waters under their land
challenger: City of Columbia, asserting a right to extract and sell the water
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that the City's proposed use of groundwater was unreasonable and could be enjoined if it injured the landowners' beneficial use.
principle: Property rights in percolating groundwater are subject to a rule of reasonable use, balancing the rights of overlying landowners against other beneficial uses, and rejecting absolute ownership.
doctrines: Reasonable Use Doctrine; Percolating Waters; Eminent Domain; Injunction

case_name: Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.
property_holder: Spur Industries Inc., in its feedlot operation
challenger: Del E. Webb Development Co., on behalf of its residents
owner_prevailed_why: The owner's operation was enjoined, but the owner received compensation for the forced relocation.
principle: Courts can use equitable powers to fashion remedies that balance the rights of a lawful but polluting business with the public's right to be free from nuisance, even requiring compensation for relocation.
doctrines: Public Nuisance; Coming to the Nuisance; Equitable Relief; Locality Rule

plaintiff: Josephine Skendzel, Jean Legowski and Bernice Wysocki
defendant: Agnes P. Marshall, Charles P. Marshall and Anna J. Blair
property_holder: Skendzel, Legowski, Wysocki, in the land as vendor-assignees
challenger: Marshall, asserting an equitable interest in the land
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the vendee's equitable interest by requiring judicial foreclosure instead of forfeiture.
principle: Courts will use equitable powers to prevent unconscionable forfeitures in land sale contracts, treating them as secured transactions akin to mortgages.
doctrines: Equity abhors forfeitures; Liquidated damages vs. penalty; Land sale contract as secured transaction; Judicial foreclosure

plaintiff: Dr. Edward L. Eyerman et al.
defendant: Mercantile Trust Co., N.A., et al.
property_holder: Louise Woodruff Johnston, in her house and land
challenger: neighboring property owners and subdivision trustees
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the community's interest and the estate's value over the deceased owner's destructive testamentary instruction.
principle: Testamentary freedom to destroy property is limited by public policy considerations, especially when the destruction is capricious and causes significant harm to the community and the estate.
doctrines: Public Policy; Testamentary Freedom; Right to Destroy; Standing

case_name: Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel
property_holder: Township of Mount Laurel, in its zoning power over land within its boundaries
challenger: low and moderate-income families and organizations representing them
owner_prevailed_why: The court found the township's zoning ordinance to be exclusionary and therefore invalid, requiring it to provide opportunities for low and moderate-income housing.
principle: Municipal zoning power must serve the general welfare, which includes a regional obligation to provide a fair share of affordable housing, and cannot be used to exclude residents based on income.
doctrines: Exclusionary Zoning; General Welfare Doctrine; Fair Share Doctrine; Substantive Due Process

property_holder: Holbrook, in his land
challenger: Taylor, asserting a right to use a roadway
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Taylors' interest in using the roadway due to their reliance and improvements, despite the Holbrooks' ownership of the land.
principle: Equitable estoppel can transform a revocable license into an irrevocable right to use another's land when the licensee has made substantial expenditures in reliance on the license.
doctrines: Easement by Estoppel; Irrevocable License; Easement by Prescription; Equitable Estoppel

property_holder: Blackett, in the residential apartments
challenger: Olanoff, as residential tenants
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the landlords breached the implied warranty of quiet enjoyment, allowing the tenants to vacate without paying rent.
principle: A landlord's implied warranty of quiet enjoyment can be breached by conditions created by another tenant if the landlord has the ability to control those conditions.
doctrines: Implied Warranty of Quiet Enjoyment; Constructive Eviction; Landlord Control Over Nuisance

class_topic: Entity Forms: Condos, Coops, Corps, Partnerships & Trusts
property_holder: Mark Rothko's estate, in his paintings
challenger: the executors and Marlborough corporations
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the estate's interest by removing disloyal executors, rescinding wrongful contracts, and awarding appreciation damages.
principle: Fiduciaries must act with undivided loyalty to the property owner's interests, and breaches of this duty, especially those involving self-dealing, will be met with strict remedies designed to fully restore the owner.
doctrines: Duty of Loyalty; No Further Inquiry Rule; Appreciation Damages; Executor's Duty of Prudence

class_topic: Criminal Law, Self-Help & Common Law Defenses
property_holder: Wiley, the landlord, in the leased restaurant premises
challenger: Wiley, asserting a right to retake possession
owner_prevailed_why: The landlord's self-help lockout was held wrongful; owners must use judicial process to retake possession, even from a tenant in breach.
principle: A landlord cannot use self-help to evict a tenant who has not abandoned or voluntarily surrendered the premises; judicial process is the exclusive remedy.
doctrines: Wrongful Eviction; Self-Help Repossession; Forcible Entry and Unlawful Detainer

case_name: Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City
court: Supreme Court of the United States
plaintiff: Penn Central Transportation Co. et al.
property_holder: Penn Central Transportation Co., in Grand Central Terminal and its air rights
challenger: New York City's Landmarks Preservation Law
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the law did not constitute a taking because it allowed reasonable beneficial use of the property and did not interfere with distinct investment-backed expectations.
principle: Government regulations that restrict property use for public benefit do not constitute a taking if they allow reasonable beneficial use of the property as a whole and do not interfere with distinct investment-backed expectations.
doctrines: Regulatory Takings; Ad Hoc Factual Inquiry; Parcel as a Whole; Transferable Development Rights

property_holder: Delfino and Vealencis, as tenants in common of the land
challenger: Delfino, seeking to force a sale of the property
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected Vealencis's interest in continued possession and livelihood, but did not deny the Delfinos' right to partition.
principle: Courts prioritize partition in kind for co-owned property, especially when one owner has a long-standing possessory interest and livelihood tied to the land, over a partition by sale that would disrupt such interests.
doctrines: Partition in Kind; Partition by Sale; Tenancy in Common; Burden of Proof

defendant: Charles L. Ruperto and Edith C. Ruperto, and Tom McCormick
property_holder: Ruperto and McCormick, in the adjacent lot
challenger: Carpenter, asserting adverse possession
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the record owners' interest by denying the adverse possession claim due to the possessor's lack of good faith.
principle: Adverse possession requires a good faith claim of right, which is absent when the possessor knows they have no legal right to the property.
doctrines: Adverse Possession; Claim of Right; Good Faith

class_topic: Criminal Law, Self-Help & Common Law Defenses
case_name: Williams v. Ford Motor Credit Co.
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
property_holder: Cathy Williams, in her car
challenger: Ford Motor Credit Company, asserting a right to repossess
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the secured party's right to repossess without judicial process was not violated.
principle: Self-help repossession is permissible under the UCC as long as it does not involve a breach of the peace, which generally requires more than mere confrontation if the debtor does not actively object or resist.
doctrines: Self-Help Repossession; Breach of the Peace; Conversion; UCC Article 9

property_holder: Allen, in her automobile
challenger: Hyatt Regency-Nashville Hotel, by denying liability for theft
owner_prevailed_why: The court found a bailment existed, making the hotel liable for the theft of the owner's car.
principle: Courts may interpret traditional property concepts like bailment flexibly to align with modern commercial realities and consumer expectations regarding the protection of property.
doctrines: Bailment for Hire; Implied Bailment; Presumption of Negligence

property_holder: Florence Gillmor, Edward Leslie Gillmor, and C. Frank Gillmor, in their undivided interests as tenants in common
challenger: Florence Gillmor, asserting her right to use the common property
owner_prevailed_why: Florence Gillmor, as a cotenant, prevailed in her claim for damages due to ouster, but the defendant cotenant was allowed an offset for necessary repairs.
principle: While cotenants generally have a right to use the entire common property without liability, one cotenant can be liable for ouster if they actively prevent another cotenant from exercising their right to use the property after a clear demand.
doctrines: Tenancy in Common; Ouster; Contribution for Repairs; Exclusive Use

defendant: Charles D. Sprague, Carl T. Simmons, Mary E. Simmons
property_holder: William Harms and John Harms, as joint tenants
challenger: Charles Sprague (as devisee) and Carl and Mary Simmons (as mortgagees)
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected William Harms' right of survivorship as the remaining joint tenant, finding the mortgage did not sever the tenancy and was extinguished upon the mortgagor's death.
principle: The effect of an encumbrance on a joint tenancy depends on whether the jurisdiction views the encumbrance as a lien or a transfer of title.
doctrines: Joint Tenancy; Right of Survivorship; Lien Theory of Mortgages; Severance

case_name: Mullendore Theatres Inc. v. Growth Realty Investors Co.
property_holder: Growth Realty Investors Co., in the leased property
challenger: Mullendore Theatres, Inc., asserting a claim to the security deposit
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the covenant to refund the security deposit did not bind the successor landlord.
principle: For a covenant to run with the land and bind successors, it must directly affect the physical use or value of the land, not merely be a personal financial obligation.
doctrines: Covenant Running with the Land; Touch and Concern Test; Collateral and Personal Obligation; Promise to Pay Money

case_name: Warsaw v. Chicago Metallic Ceilings Inc.
property_holder: Chicago Metallic Ceilings, Inc., in its fee simple land
challenger: Warsaw, asserting a prescriptive easement
owner_prevailed_why: The court recognized a prescriptive easement over the owner's land and ordered the owner to remove an encroaching structure without compensation.
principle: Prescriptive easements, once established, do not require compensation to the burdened landowner, and willful encroachments interfering with such easements must be removed.
doctrines: Prescriptive Easement; Mandatory Injunction; Willful Encroachment; Equitable Discretion

plaintiff: Richard S. Murphy and Beatrice K. Murphy
property_holder: The Murphys, in their home
challenger: Financial Development Corporation and Colonial Deposit Company, through foreclosure
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Murphys' equity interest by finding the lenders breached their duty of due diligence, but limited the damages and denied attorney's fees.
principle: Mortgagees exercising a power of sale owe a fiduciary-like duty of due diligence to the mortgagor to obtain a fair price, even if statutory notice requirements are met.
doctrines: Power of Sale Mortgage; Duty of Good Faith; Duty of Due Diligence; Fiduciary Duty

court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
property_holder: Stalnaker, in his land
challenger: Hendricks, asserting a right to use his adjacent land for a septic system
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected Stalnaker's right to use his land for a water well, finding it was not an unreasonable use despite its impact on his neighbor.
principle: A private nuisance claim requires a showing that the defendant's interference with the plaintiff's land use is unreasonable, which is determined by balancing the gravity of the harm against the social utility of the defendant's conduct.
doctrines: Private Nuisance; Intentional Interference; Unreasonable Interference; Balancing Test

case_name: Moore v. Regents of the University of California
defendant: The Regents of the University of California et al.
property_holder: Moore, in his excised cells
challenger: The Regents of the University of California, Golde, Quan, Genetics Institute, Sandoz, asserting ownership and use rights over the cell line
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that Moore did not retain a property interest in his excised cells sufficient to support a conversion claim.
principle: Property rights in one's own body are limited, particularly when tissues are removed and transformed through scientific labor into new, patentable creations, but patients retain rights to informed consent regarding the commercial interests of their physicians.
doctrines: Conversion; Informed Consent; Fiduciary Duty; Patent Law

class_topic: Entity Forms: Condos, Coops, Corps, Partnerships & Trusts
case_name: Levandusky v. One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.
property_holder: Levandusky, in his apartment and its fixtures
challenger: One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp., asserting its right to enforce building policy
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld the cooperative board's decision to prevent the alteration, limiting the individual owner's right to modify his property.
principle: The governance of cooperative and condominium associations is subject to a deferential standard of judicial review, akin to the business judgment rule, which prioritizes the collective interests of the community over individual owner autonomy.
doctrines: Business Judgment Rule; Cooperative Board Authority; Reasonableness Standard; Arbitrary and Capricious Standard

property_holder: Miles Postema, in his law degree
challenger: Kathryn Postema, asserting an equitable claim against the value of the degree
owner_prevailed_why: The court recognized an equitable claim by the non-degree-earning spouse against the value of the degree, requiring compensation.
principle: Courts may recognize equitable claims against non-traditional assets like professional degrees in divorce, focusing on compensating for contributions rather than valuing the asset itself.
doctrines: Equitable Distribution; Marital Asset; Concerted Family Effort; Equitable Claim

chapter: 8. Title Records and the Transfer of Property
class_topic: Title & Transfer: Land Transactions, Good Faith Purchasers & Recording
property_holder: Nowlin Jewelry, Inc., in the Rolex watch
challenger: Kotis, asserting a claim of good faith purchase
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that Kotis was not a good faith purchaser, thus Nowlin Jewelry retained title to the watch.
area: 8. Title Records and the Transfer of Property
principle: A buyer cannot acquire good title from a seller with voidable title if the buyer fails to act in good faith, especially when suspicious circumstances are present.
doctrines: Voidable Title; Good Faith Purchaser; UCC 2.403; Honesty in Fact

case_name: Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council
court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: Lucas, in his two beachfront lots
challenger: South Carolina Coastal Council, through the Beachfront Management Act
owner_prevailed_why: The Court held that the regulation constituted a categorical taking because it deprived Lucas of all economically beneficial use of his land, and the state failed to show the prohibited use was already unlawful under background principles of property and nuisance law.
principle: Government regulations that eliminate all economically beneficial use of private property constitute a compensable taking, unless the prohibited use was already restricted by pre-existing property or nuisance law.
doctrines: Regulatory Takings; Total Deprivation Rule; Nuisance Exception; Just Compensation

defendant: Estate of G.A. Williams, et al.
property_holder: G.A. Williams, in the home farm
challenger: Ethel Williams, asserting a fee simple interest
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the testator's intended disposition of a limited estate, rather than an absolute fee simple for the daughters.
principle: The specific language and predominant intent of a testator in a will can create a determinable life estate, overriding general presumptions for a fee simple.
doctrines: Will Construction; Determinable Life Estate; Executory Interest; Reversion

court: Court of Appeal of the State of California
defendant: The Superior Court of Los Angeles County
property_holder: William E. Kane, in his cryogenically preserved sperm
challenger: William E. Kane, Jr., and Katharine E. Kane (decedent's children)
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the decedent's testamentary intent regarding his sperm by vacating the order for its destruction.
principle: Genetic material intended for reproduction, even after death, is a unique form of property subject to the donor's testamentary intent, and courts should not impose public policy restrictions on its use without clear legislative guidance.
doctrines: Probate Law; Property Rights in Human Tissue; Public Policy

court: United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York
property_holder: Gotlieb and Blaymore, as landlords of the commercial property
challenger: Taco Bell, by repudiating the lease
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the landlords' interest in accrued rent and the value of the unbuilt structure, but limited their claim for future rent due to their actions implying acceptance of surrender.
principle: A landlord's conduct can imply acceptance of a tenant's lease surrender, even if explicitly rejected, thereby limiting the tenant's future liability.
doctrines: Surrender by Operation of Law; Landlord's Duty to Mitigate; Liquidated Damages; Prevailing Party

class_topic: Entity Forms: Condos, Coops, Corps, Partnerships & Trusts
case_name: Nahrstedt v. Lakeside Village Condominium Association
defendant: Lakeside Village Condominium Association, Inc., et al.
property_holder: Nahrstedt, in her condominium unit
challenger: Lakeside Village Condominium Association, asserting the pet restriction
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld the condominium association's pet restriction against the individual owner's challenge.
principle: Courts generally uphold recorded covenants in common interest developments unless they are arbitrary, violate public policy, or impose burdens disproportionate to their benefits to the community as a whole.
doctrines: Equitable Servitudes; Presumption of Validity; Unreasonableness Test; Common Interest Development Act

case_name: Pocono Springs Civic Association v. MacKenzie
defendant: Joseph W. MacKenzie and Doris C. MacKenzie
property_holder: MacKenzies, in their fee simple lot
challenger: Pocono Springs Civic Association, seeking payment of fees
owner_prevailed_why: The court held that the MacKenzies could not abandon their fee simple interest to escape their obligations.
principle: Fee simple ownership of real property cannot be abandoned, meaning owners cannot unilaterally divest themselves of title and associated obligations.
doctrines: Abandonment; Fee Simple; Real Property

court: United States Court of Appeals, Seventh Circuit
defendant: Matthew Zeidenberg and Silken Mountain Web Services, Inc.
property_holder: ProCD, in its database and software
challenger: Zeidenberg, by reselling the data in violation of the license
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld ProCD's contractual right to restrict the use of its software and data, despite challenges based on contract formation and federal preemption.
principle: Contractual agreements, even those presented after payment in a 'shrinkwrap' format, can create enforceable restrictions on the use of intellectual property and are generally not preempted by federal copyright law.
doctrines: Contract Formation; UCC Article 2; Copyright Preemption; Shrinkwrap Licenses

plaintiff: Harvey F. Jacque and Lois C. Jacque
property_holder: Jacques, in their land
challenger: Steenberg Homes, asserting a right to cross the land for convenience
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Jacques' right to exclude by reinstating a large punitive damage award for intentional trespass.
principle: The right to exclude is a fundamental property right, and its intentional violation, even without measurable economic harm, can warrant significant punitive damages to deter future misconduct.
doctrines: Right to Exclude; Intentional Trespass; Punitive Damages; Nominal Damages

court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
property_holder: Navajo Nation, in the Yei B'Chei
challenger: Richard Corrow, asserting individual alienability of the Yei B'Chei
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld the conviction, affirming that the Yei B'Chei were cultural patrimony and inalienable by an individual.
principle: Statutes can redefine property rights to protect culturally significant items from individual alienation, even if traditional notions of ownership are complex or disputed within the cultural group.
doctrines: Cultural Patrimony; Void-for-Vagueness Doctrine; Scienter Requirement; Strict Liability

property_holder: Adams, in their land
challenger: Cleveland-Cliffs Iron Co., through its mining operations
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that the plaintiffs' claim did not meet the legal definition of trespass, thus denying their recovery under that theory.
principle: The court maintains a strict distinction between trespass and nuisance, requiring a direct, physical, and tangible intrusion for trespass, while intangible interferences fall under nuisance.
doctrines: Trespass; Nuisance; Tangible Object Requirement; Direct Intrusion Requirement

chapter: 8. Title Records and the Transfer of Property
class_topic: Title & Transfer: Land Transactions, Good Faith Purchasers & Recording
property_holder: Wood, in the legal title to the house
challenger: Donohue, asserting equitable ownership
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that Wood's legal title was merely a security interest and that Donohue, as equitable owner, was entitled to the settlement funds.
area: 8. Title Records and the Transfer of Property
principle: The doctrine of equitable conversion dictates that the beneficial ownership of real property transfers to the buyer upon the formation of a contract for sale, making the buyer responsible for losses and entitled to benefits.
doctrines: Equitable Conversion; Land Installment Contract; Equitable Owner; Vendor's Lien

plaintiff: James G. Schwab and Katherine Schwab, Dorice McCormick
defendant: Helen Timmons, Carl D. Lenz Trust, et al.
property_holder: Respondents, in their parcels of land
challenger: Petitioners, asserting a right-of-way over the respondents' land
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the respondents' property interests by denying the petitioners' claim for an easement.
principle: Courts disfavor implied easements, particularly when they are self-created or would undermine the integrity of the recording system and settled expectations of landowners.
doctrines: Easement by Necessity; Easement by Implication; Recording Acts; Notice

case_name: Songbyrd Inc. v. Estate of Grossman
court: United States Court of Appeals, Second Circuit
property_holder: SongByrd, Inc., as successor-in-interest to Henry Roeland Byrd's intellectual property rights in the master tapes
challenger: Estate of Grossman, asserting ownership by possession and licensing
owner_prevailed_why: The court found the owner's claim was time-barred due to the possessor's open acts of ownership.
principle: Statutes of limitations for conversion begin to run when a possessor openly exercises dominion over property inconsistent with the true owner's rights, even without a formal demand.
doctrines: Statute of Limitations; Conversion; Personal Jurisdiction; Accrual Rule

class_topic: Criminal Law, Self-Help & Common Law Defenses
property_holder: Intel, in its computer systems and email network
challenger: Hamidi, asserting a right to communicate with employees via the system
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that Intel's property interest in its computer system was not sufficiently harmed to constitute trespass to chattels.
principle: The tort of trespass to chattels requires actual or threatened physical damage or functional impairment to the personal property itself, not merely economic harm or annoyance caused by the content of communications transmitted through it.
doctrines: Trespass to Chattels; Actual Injury Rule; Injunctive Relief

class_topic: Entity Forms: Condos, Coops, Corps, Partnerships & Trusts
property_holder: Pullman, in his proprietary lease and shares
challenger: the cooperative corporation
owner_prevailed_why: The court upheld the cooperative's termination of Pullman's tenancy, limiting his property interest.
principle: Cooperative boards have broad discretion under the business judgment rule to manage their communities, even to the point of terminating a shareholder-tenant's lease for objectionable conduct, provided they act in good faith and within their authority.
doctrines: Business Judgment Rule; Proprietary Lease; Objectionable Conduct; RPAPL 711 (1)

case_name: Kelo v. City of New London
court: Supreme Court of the United States
defendant: City of New London et al.
property_holder: Kelo et al., in their homes and investment properties
challenger: City of New London, asserting eminent domain for economic development
owner_prevailed_why: The court ruled that the city's economic development plan constituted a valid public use, allowing the taking of the owners' properties.
principle: The government's power of eminent domain, under the 'public use' clause, extends to taking private property for economic development purposes, even if transferred to other private entities, so long as it serves a public purpose.
doctrines: Public Use; Eminent Domain; Economic Development Takings; Deference to Legislative Judgment

court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: MercExchange, in its patent rights
challenger: eBay, by infringing the patent
owner_prevailed_why: The court affirmed the patent holder's right to seek an injunction but required application of a flexible equitable standard, not an automatic injunction.
principle: The availability of injunctive relief for property rights, including intellectual property, is subject to traditional equitable discretion and a four-factor test, not automatic entitlement.
doctrines: Permanent Injunction; Equitable Discretion; Patent Infringement

class_topic: Entity Forms: Condos, Coops, Corps, Partnerships & Trusts
case_name: Kiekel v. Four Colonies Homes Association
property_holder: Kiekels, in their rental properties
challenger: Four Colonies Homes Association, asserting new rental restrictions
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the Kiekels' right to rent their properties by invalidating the bylaw amendment that sought to restrict it.
principle: New restrictions on fundamental property rights in common interest communities must be enacted through proper amendment procedures of the primary governing document (Declaration), not through less stringent bylaw amendments.
doctrines: Restrictive Covenants; Declaration vs. Bylaws; Amendment Authority; Strict Construction

case_name: Stop the Beach Renourishment Inc. v. Florida Department of Environmental Protection
court: Supreme Court of the United States
property_holder: The beachfront property owners, in their littoral rights (right to accretions, right to contact with water)
challenger: The State of Florida, through its beach restoration project and the Florida Supreme Court's interpretation of property rights
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that the Florida Supreme Court's decision did not eliminate an established property right under state law.
principle: A state court's reinterpretation of property law can be a compensable taking under the Fifth Amendment if it eliminates an established private property right, but courts must defer to state law in defining those rights.
doctrines: Judicial Takings; Takings Clause; Accretion and Avulsion; State Property Law

court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
property_holder: Marrow donors, in their own bone-marrow cells
challenger: Plaintiffs seeking to compensate donors for certain cells
owner_prevailed_why: Donors may be paid for marrow cells collected from the bloodstream, but the ban on paying for aspirated marrow stands.
principle: Statutes regulating property interests, especially those involving new technologies, are interpreted based on ordinary meaning and legislative intent at the time of enactment, rather than extending to analogous but distinct practices.
doctrines: Statutory Interpretation; Commodification; Equal Protection

case_name: Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommate.com LLC
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
plaintiff: Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley; The Fair Housing Council of San Diego
property_holder: Roommate.com users, in their right to choose roommates for their homes
challenger: Fair Housing Councils, asserting anti-discrimination laws
owner_prevailed_why: The court protected the users' right to choose roommates by interpreting anti-discrimination statutes not to apply to shared living situations.
principle: The government's power to regulate property use is limited by constitutional rights, particularly the right to intimate association and privacy within the home.
doctrines: Fair Housing Act; Right to Intimate Association; Canon of Constitutional Avoidance; FEHA

property_holder: Scott, in the disputed twenty acres of land
challenger: Anderson-Tully Company, claiming adverse possession
owner_prevailed_why: The court found that Anderson-Tully Company successfully established all elements of adverse possession, thereby extinguishing Scott's title.
principle: Adverse possession allows for the transfer of title to land when a non-owner openly, notoriously, and continuously possesses the property for a statutory period, especially when the land is unimproved.
doctrines: Adverse Possession; Claim of Ownership; Hostile Possession; Open and Notorious Possession
